settings.content: Quarter, half, three-quarter or full, and what each commits you to

settings.eyebrow: The Decision That Changes Everything Else
settings.heading: Settle Coverage First
settings.body:
Coverage is the single decision that changes an eternity ring most: how much sparkle you see, how the ring feels, what it costs, and how much can be altered later. Everything else is easier to decide once coverage is settled.

One thing to know before the table below. Coverage names are useful descriptions rather than a guarantee of an exact visual result. Stone diameter, finger size, setting and stone count all affect how far the set section appears to travel around the finger.

settings.cells: Quarter, around 25% | A light accent | Plain metal beneath | Usually possible within limits | Lowest
Third, around 33% | A clear line | Plain metal beneath | Usually possible within limits | Low to middle
Half, around 50% | Reads as covered from above | Smooth plain underside | Often possible, setting dependent | Middle
Three-quarter, around 75% | Sparkle from most angles | Small plain section remains | More limited | Higher
Full, 100% | Uninterrupted, every angle | Stones and settings beneath | Usually not possible | Highest

settings.note: Partial-coverage rings can rotate. A correct fit, balanced construction and enough side coverage all help, but no partial ring is completely immune to movement.
settings.heading: Coverage Compared
settings.headers: Coverage | Visible sparkle | Comfort beneath | Conventional resizing | Relative cost

settings.heading: Half Is Not a Compromise
settings.body:
The arc you actually see is roughly the top 120 degrees of the band, viewed from above at arm's length. A half-eternity sets 180 degrees of stones, which comfortably exceeds that visible arc. This is why half coverage reads as covered.

From ordinary viewing angles a well-proportioned half-eternity can look remarkably similar to a full one, for a lower price, a smoother underside and far more future flexibility. It is the practical sweet spot for most wearers, not the budget option.

settings.heading: Check it on a hand, not a stand
settings.body: Ask for a photograph of the ring worn rather than shot on a stand. A set section that looks wide enough in a product image may expose plain metal once the ring rotates.

settings.heading: Finger size changes the maths
settings.body: On a larger finger the same 180 degrees of stones covers proportionally less of the hand's silhouette. Check coverage against the actual size rather than the product photograph.

settings.heading: Plain metal is useful
settings.body: The underside gives a jeweller somewhere to adjust, engrave or repair. Extensive settings still limit what is safe, but some plain metal is always better than none.

settings.heading: Rotation is a fit problem first
settings.body: A ring that spins is often a weight-distribution issue rather than a coverage one. Sizing beads frequently solve it without changing the design at all.

settings.heading: Quarter, Third and Half in Practice

settings.label: Sizing is usually permanent
settings.note: A significant size change may require partial rebuilding or remaking entirely.

settings.label: Specification changes with size
settings.note: Exact carat weight and stone count differ between sizes, so two sizes of the same design are not identical rings.

settings.label: Stones sit beneath the finger
settings.note: They meet keys, handles and work surfaces, and collect more dirt than an open plain underside.

settings.label: Maintenance is higher
settings.note: Fine or exposed settings need regular inspection, and engraving space may be limited or absent.

settings.label: Records matter more
settings.note: The specification is harder to reconstruct after a loss, so insurance detail and photographs are worth keeping.

settings.label: Choose it for the right reason
settings.note: Because you value the uninterrupted design, not because it is assumed to be the best version.

settings.intro: A full-eternity ring is beautiful and looks finished from every angle. It also asks for more certainty than any other band we make.
settings.heading: The Full-Eternity Commitment
Size Certainty Comes Before Full Coverage
settings.body: If there is any doubt about the finger size, a half or three-quarter eternity is the calmer route. We will only recommend a full eternity when we are confident in the size, and we would rather say so than sell you something that cannot be adjusted.

settings.q: Is a half-eternity ring worth it compared with a full one?
settings.a: For most people, yes. The visible arc of a ring viewed normally is around the top 120 degrees, and a half-eternity sets 180 degrees, so it reads as covered from ordinary angles. You get a smoother underside, a lower price and the ability to resize later.

settings.q: Can a full-eternity ring be resized?
settings.a: Usually not in the conventional way. There is nowhere to cut and no plain metal to add or remove. A significant size change means partial rebuilding or remaking, which is why we insist on size certainty before making one.

settings.q: Why does my eternity ring keep spinning?
settings.a: Usually fit or weight distribution rather than coverage. If the stones are all on top, the ring is top-heavy and will rotate. Sizing beads or a small shank adjustment normally solve it without altering the design.

settings.q: Do two sizes of the same full-eternity ring have the same carat weight?
settings.a: No. A larger size needs more stones, or larger ones, so the total carat weight and stone count both change. This is why quoted carat weights on full-eternity rings are often approximate.

settings.q: Is it uncomfortable having stones under the finger?
settings.a: Most people adjust quickly, but it is a real difference. Stones and settings beneath the finger meet keys, handles and work surfaces, and collect more dirt than plain metal. If you work with your hands, three-quarter coverage is the sensible compromise.
